title: Duke Ellington's offer and Arthur Whetsol's chops
summary: Ellington, hearing Briggs at Bricktop's, invited him to join; Briggs refused partly because the heavy brass writing had worn out Arthur Whetsol.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: And it was during one of those evenings that the great Duke came into Bricktop's, which was the headquarters of every who's who, as I was saying.
And it was during that one evening that someone, a client had asked -- I said a client, that's not the word --
A client had asked for that number, "Dein, ist mein ganzist herz." "You Are My Heart's Delight".
And I played it for him and Duke, I don't know -- Duke was there, and he heard me play it, and he asked me, whether I'd be interested to come with him.
I told him, I preferred to be here, because I just one thing -- in any case, even if I was broke and out of a job, I would never take it, because it was Art Whetsol's job, rhythm.
Chief. Art Whetsol was with him. and he was blown to death by Duke's orchestra, and I know, because Art was a personal friend that I met.
You mean his chops were all messed up.
His chops were all messed up.
Yeh, and he was ready to kill me, but I wasn't in for the killing (Laughter).
Well, Duke, would what, wear out those first trumpet players.
And he's not the only one. There were quite a few of them. You see those men, those are orchestra leaders that don't know what trympet playing is, or brass playing is, they just want to kill you.
Right. He used that brass a lot, too, Duke.
And he wrote, and he wrote. His writing, he writes puzzles sort of brass. I mean he'll kill you. You'll keep blowing for almost a half hour, straight, an hour without a break.
